posts.title: How the broth gets inside
posts.excerpt: A look behind the glass wall at how roasted bones, aromatics, and patient chilling turn rich broth into firm jelly cubes ready for the fold.
posts.content:
Guests standing in the queue along 12 Harbour Street often look through the glass wall and ask the same question: how does hot, liquid soup end up sealed inside a steamed dumpling without breaking the delicate wrapper? The answer lies not in liquid injections or complex pastry tricks, but in a disciplined daily routine of slow reduction, natural gelatin extraction, and temperature control that begins before sunrise in Port Aldren.

Every batch of broth starts with co-founder Samuel Adeyemi at our Harbour Street kitchen. Simmered slowly over several hours with sliced ginger, scallions, and pork bones, the stock extracts rich collagen until it turns dense, golden, and deeply fragrant. Once strained through fine mesh, the liquid broth is poured into shallow stainless steel trays and transferred to our walk-in coolers to rest overnight. As the broth cools overnight in our coolers, the rich gelatin sets into a clear, firm jelly that can be sliced cleanly with a prep knife.

By 06:30 each morning, the broth jelly is completely set and doughs have finished resting. Kitchen lead Priya Raman and her team slice the cold sheets into precise small cubes on the steel prep bench. These chilled cubes are immediately folded into seasoned minced meat—either pork, chicken, or crab—ensuring an exact proportion throughout the mixture. When co-founder Lena Kowal and the folding crew take their stations at the glass counter, every single dumpling is weighed on the counter scale: exactly six grams of rested wheat wrapper and fifteen grams of filling with its embedded broth jelly, bringing the total pre-steamed dumpling to precisely twenty-one grams.

Keeping the ingredients cold is essential to the craft. If the kitchen bench becomes too warm, the broth jelly softens prematurely, soaking into the six-gram wrapper and making the dough impossible to pleat. Working quickly with floured fingers, each cook gathers the wrapper into eighteen uniform folds, twisting the top into a tight crown that seals the filling and jelly completely within the dough pocket.

The final transformation happens inside the bamboo steamer. When an order arrives from the front counter, the basket is placed over rolling boiling water for exactly seven minutes. Inside the sealed bamboo chamber, intense steam cooks the raw meat while completely melting the broth jelly back into its liquid state. Because the eighteen pleats form a reinforced, airtight seal, the wrapper balloons slightly without bursting, capturing every drop of aromatic broth inside.

When Tomasz Nowak hands the steaming basket across to your table or takeaway window, that melted jelly has become the piping-hot soup waiting inside. Eating it requires a moment of care: lift the dumpling onto a soup spoon, nibble a tiny opening in the wrapper near the crown to release the initial steam, sip the soup, and enjoy the result of seven minutes of steam and hours of patient morning preparation.

Broth is simmered with ginger and bones, strained and chilled overnight.

By 06:30 it has set into a jelly that is cut into cubes and folded into the filling.

Seven minutes in the steamer melt the jelly back into soup inside eighteen folds.

posts.title: A table for six at Harbour Street
posts.excerpt: Six friends share baskets at a wooden table on Harbour Street, hands reaching across the steamers.
posts.content:
The long table at the back of the Harbour Street kitchen seats six, close enough to the glass to watch the bench. Tomasz Nowak sets it with a dish of black vinegar and ginger on the house, and a pot of jasmine tea at €3.50.

A table of six usually orders three baskets of pork, one of mushroom and greens, and a round of garlic greens, then passes them around. The baskets arrive one at a time, straight from the steamer.

The long table at the back of Harbour Street seats six, close to the glass.

Six usually order three pork baskets, one mushroom and greens, and garlic greens.

Black vinegar and ginger come with the table; the jasmine tea pot is €3.50.

posts.title: Morning: the first two thousand wrappers
posts.excerpt: Wrappers are rolled to six grams on the bench before the doors open.
posts.content:
At 08:00 the doughs have rested and the rolling begins. Each wrapper is rolled by hand to six grams, thin at the edge and thicker in the middle so it can carry the filling and the broth.

By 10:30 the first folds are pleated behind the glass, and by 11:00, when the doors open, there are two thousand wrappers on the bench waiting for the day.

The doughs have rested by 08:00 and the rolling begins.

Each wrapper is rolled by hand to six grams.

By 11:00 there are two thousand wrappers on the bench.
